entities.summary:
The Labour Party of the United Kingdom, founded in 1900 by a coalition of trade unions and socialist societies, is one of the world's most significant social democratic parties — governing Britain during its most transformative periods: Clement Attlee's post-war government (1945-1951) created the National Health Service, nationalized major industries, and built the British welfare state; Harold Wilson presided over the 1960s cultural revolution; Tony Blair's New Labour won three consecutive landslide victories (1997-2010). Labour's founding represented the entry of the organized working class into British parliamentary politics.

Labour was created from the 1900 Labour Representation Committee, a coalition of trade union delegates and socialist organizations (Fabian Society, Independent Labour Party, Social Democratic Federation). Keir Hardie, a Scottish miner who had entered Parliament bareheaded (defying the top hat convention), was its first leader. Labour replaced the Liberal Party as the primary alternative to the Conservatives by 1922, accelerating British political realignment.

Attlee's 1945 landslide against Churchill — despite Churchill's wartime popularity — reflected working-class Britain's determination to prevent a return to the 1930s unemployment and poverty. The Attlee government's creation of the NHS (1948), nationalization of coal, steel, railways, and utilities, and establishment of the welfare state represented the most transformative domestic program in 20th-century British history. Blair's 1997 New Labour landslide was the party's greatest electoral victory, while Jeremy Corbyn's leadership (2015-2020) and Keir Starmer's 2024 landslide represent the party's ideological range.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Labour Party's creation of the National Health Service in 1948 — free healthcare for all at point of need — is the most consequential domestic policy achievement in British history and became the model for universal healthcare worldwide.
